title: Chennai's Indian Fine Arts Society Honours Its Young Carnatic Stars
excerpt: More than 20 children took prizes at the 93-year-old sabha's annual music competition, with top winners receiving Thanjavur tamburas at a ceremony in Alwarpet on Sunday.
body:
• The Indian Fine Arts Society, a 93-year-old Chennai sabha, closed its annual student music competition with a prize ceremony at Ethiraja Kalyana Nilayam, Alwarpet, on Sunday.
  • Over 75 children competed in junior and senior categories on September 19; more than 20 received prizes, with first-prize winners in the Thyagarajar and Muthuswami Dikshithar krithi categories awarded Thanjavur tamburas.
  • Noted vocalist Dr. N. Vijay Siva — himself a former IFAS competitor in the 1980s — handed over the prizes and urged the young musicians to cherish the friendships forged in competition and stay rooted in Indian culture.

Opening lead

The next generation of Carnatic musicians took center stage in Chennai on Sunday, as the Indian Fine Arts Society — one of the city's oldest sabhas at 93 — felicitated the winners of its annual student music competition at Ethiraja Kalyana Nilayam in Alwarpet.

Context & Background

More than 75 children competed in junior and senior categories on September 19, performing before a jury of veteran musicians after registration and preliminary rounds. Over 20 children received prizes, and the first-prize winners in the Thyagarajar and Muthuswami Dikshithar krithi categories were awarded Thanjavur tamburas — the traditional drone instrument that is a Carnatic musician's most prized possession.

Prizes were handed over by noted vocalist Dr. N. Vijay Siva, who told the gathering he had himself competed in the same IFAS competition in the 1980s — "never then did I even imagine that one day I would be distributing the prizes." He praised the sabha's management for organizing the competition every year, noting the volunteers, registrations, and coordination it demands.

"More than participation and prizes, you must remember that the friendship that you cultivate with other competing children is forever and you must cherish it all your life. You should always stand firmly rooted in the essence of Indian culture."

— Dr. N. Vijay Siva

Impact & Analysis

The prize ceremony capped a weekend steeped in the Carnatic canon. On Sunday, young artists presented Muthuswami Dikshithar krithis — Srijith Poosarla on mandolin, Shreeya Ananth on violin, Anghiras Mahadevan on mridangam, and Shrinidhi Raghunandan on kanjira — followed by an evening veena concert by Dr. Nithyashree, accompanied by Poongulam Balasubramanian on mridangam and B. S. Purushothaman on kanjira. Friday's programs featured GNB, Swathi Thirunal, and Papanasam Sivan krithis; Saturday's honored Shyama Sastri, Annamacharya, and Purandaradasa.

In his welcome address, IFAS president K.V. Ramachandran congratulated the winners and praised parents for encouraging their children to pursue classical music. Vice president K. Venkatrangam proposed the vote of thanks, and honorary secretary Dr. R. Radhakrishnan also addressed the gathering.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs, the competition is a window into the pipeline that feeds Chennai's famed December music season. Families planning Margazhi-season trips can expect to see today's prize-winners on tomorrow's concert stages — and parents raising children on Carnatic lessons abroad get a reminder of the ecosystem of competitions, sabhas, and gurus that keeps the tradition thriving back home.

What's Next

With the competition season done, Chennai's sabhas now turn toward the Margazhi music festival in December and January, when many of these young musicians will get their first taste of the season's concert circuit.
